To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the steroidogenic action PTTH is dependent on calcium entry into the prothoracotic gland cell.
calcium entry is required for PTTH action and that this calcium entry may be mediated by a calcium channel.
PTTH stimulates ecdysone release in pupal prohoracic glands by increasing calcium entry into the cell, possibly by opening a calcium channel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of a presumptive PTTH-stimulating calcium pathway in the steroidogenic prothoracic gland of the tobacco horn worm.
the identification of the mechanisms involved in the calcium mobilization that is necessary for PTTH-stimulatd cAMP production in the protharoxic glands of the tobacco horworm, Manduca sext.
calcium mobilization pathways in the prothroacic glands of Manduca sextas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PTTH-stimulat-ed calcium mobilization is not due to the release of intracellular calcium stores, but rather is due to the opening of a L-type calcium channel.
PTTH stimulates ecdysone release in prothoracig glands by mobilizing calcium through the opening of an L-type calcium channel, and not by IP3-induced calcium release from intracellular stores.

the PTTH-induced mobilization of calcium is a complex process involving a G protein, but not a pertussis toxin-sensitive G protein, and that the mobilization is not mediated by inositol phosphate metabolism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

calcium entry into the prothoracig glands may occur through a calcium channel, but that calcium release from intracellular stores may occur in the prothocarcal organs, the source of PTTH, or in the central nervous system, the source of the PTTH precursor.
calcium is mobilized by PTTH via the opening of a L-type calcium channel, possibly through a G-protein-coupled mechanism.
PTTH activates the G-protein Gs, which stimulates the opening of a L-type calcium channel in the plasma membrane of the prothoracoglandular cells, resulting in an increase in cytosolic calcium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the steroidogenic action in the prothoric glands of PTTH does not require the activation of a phosphoinositide cascade, but instead is dependent on calcium influx through L-type channels.
calcium mobilization in the prothoricotrophic hormone (PTTH) response is independent of inositol triposphate (IP3)-induced release of stored calcium.
PTTH does not stimulate ecdysteroid synthesis by increasing the concentration of intracellular calcium through the release of stored calcium.
